Five Apple Watch models can measure your blood pressure and alert you to possible hypertension, but they won't give you an actual reading.

Some smart rings and other fitness devices can provide actual readings, but they need to be regularly calibrated against a traditional upper-arm blood pressure monitor. The upcoming Signal Ring claims to deliver full blood pressure measurements without any calibration, backed by clinical trials involving thousands of participants...

"The silent killer"

Abnormally high blood pressure (hypertension) and abnormally low blood pressure (hypotension) can both pose significant health risks.

Of the two, high blood pressure is more dangerous and has even been dubbed "the silent killer," because it can cause serious, irreversible damage to your arteries, heart and brain without any obvious symptoms. It often goes undetected until it triggers a heart attack or stroke.

This is especially important for older adults, who should monitor their blood pressure regularly—and home blood pressure monitors are widely available for self-checking. But being able to monitor automatically through a fitness device you're already wearing would clearly be even more ideal.

Apple Watch blood pressure feature

The launch of watchOS 26 has enabled five Apple Watch models to measure blood pressure:

  • Apple Watch Series 11
  • Apple Watch Series 10
  • Apple Watch Series 9
  • Apple Watch Ultra 3
  • Apple Watch Ultra 2

However, these models won't provide any readings—they'll only alert you when signs of potential hypertension are detected. Other devices, such as the Oura Ring, work in a similar way.

Some fitness devices on the market can indeed provide actual blood pressure readings, but they must be regularly calibrated using measurements from a blood pressure monitor.

Signal Ring

Startup Vital Signals says it has developed a smart ring that can measure blood pressure with the same accuracy as a traditional upper-arm blood pressure monitor, without any calibration needed. The product is called the Signal Ring.

According to a Bloomberg report, its CEO Tom Moss said he nearly died from undiagnosed high blood pressure, which inspired him to start the company.

The ring will be available for pre-order later today, ship in October, and be priced at $399 with no subscription required. Real-time blood pressure readings and long-term blood pressure tracking data can be viewed through the companion app (as shown above).

It's worth noting that the Oura Ring has not yet received approval from the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA), but clinical trials have shown it delivers accurate blood pressure readings across thousands of participants.

Interestingly, Moss doesn't intend to market this ring to everyone. He says the professional feature is best suited for older adults and those assessed by a doctor as being at higher risk for hypertension—implying that the Signal Ring may be somewhat less impressive in other areas, such as sleep tracking.
